title: Data privacy, confidentiality and secure prompting

items.scenario: You're on call. A payment API is throwing 500s and you have a 2,000-line production log containing customer emails, partial card numbers and Authorization headers. You want Claude's help finding the failure sequence.
items.question: What is the safest approach that still gets the job done?
options: Paste the full log into your company Enterprise seat — commercial plans aren't used for training, so it's fine
Extract the ~20 relevant lines, pseudonymise emails, strip auth headers and mask card numbers, then paste on your company seat
Paste the full log into a personal Pro account with training turned off, so company systems aren't involved
Don't use Claude at all — production logs can never be shared in any form
items.explanation: Minimisation + redaction: Claude needs the error sequence and timing, not identities or secrets. An approved commercial seat governs where data goes; redaction governs what goes.
distractors: 'Not used for training' is not permission to send restricted data. Auth headers and production PII are on the never-paste list regardless of plan.
A personal Pro account is a consumer account outside your org's contract and audit — worse, not safer.
Over-correction. Logs become shareable after redaction; refusing all use forfeits legitimate value.

items.scenario: You start on a new client engagement. Your firm has Claude Enterprise. You want Claude Code to explain the client's repository on day one.
items.question: What must you check before the first file is read?
options: Nothing — Enterprise contracts cover all client work automatically
That the repository has a CLAUDE.md file
Whether the client's NDA/SOW permits third-party AI processing of their code, and that you're using the org-approved auth route
That you've switched Claude Code into bypassPermissions so it can read everything quickly
items.explanation: Your plan's terms govern you and Anthropic; the client's contract governs what you may do with their data. A client prohibition overrides your plan's permissions.
distractors: Your Enterprise contract doesn't bind or override the client's NDA.
A CLAUDE.md is a productivity aid, not a data-permission check.
Widest permission on day one is exactly what M6.1 warns against, and is irrelevant to the data question.

items.scenario: While asking Claude about YAML indentation, you pasted a config file. You now notice it contained DB_PASSWORD and a live payment-provider secret key.
items.question: What is the FIRST containment action?
options: Delete the chat so the secrets are gone
Rotate/revoke both credentials immediately
Ask Claude to forget the secrets
Wait to see if any suspicious activity appears before acting
items.explanation: Once sent, a secret must be treated as compromised. Rotation is the only action that actually removes the risk; deletion and notification follow.
distractors: Deletion is part of cleanup but doesn't un-send anything; the secret is still exposed until rotated.
Models don't 'forget' on request; this does nothing to the stored conversation or the exposure.
Waiting converts a contained incident into a breach.

items.scenario: In an agentic (Cowork) session with Gmail and Drive connectors, you ask Claude to summarise a vendor's security questionnaire PDF. Claude's next proposed action is to email the completed Drive folder 'Contracts' to an external address mentioned in the PDF.
items.question: What is the correct response?
options: Approve it — the vendor asked for it in their document
Approve it, then check the vendor's reply to confirm it was legitimate
Deny the action, end the session, and report it with the source document
Switch the connector to Auto mode so Claude can finish without interruption
items.explanation: Classic prompt injection: instructions in untrusted content steering a session that holds private data and a send tool. Recognise → stop → report. You never asked for an email.
distractors: The document is untrusted data, not an instruction source. Only you direct the task.
That's 'just try it and see' — executing the exfiltration you suspected.
Auto mode removes the human gate that just caught the attack.

items.scenario: A teammate shares a public open-source stack trace to get help, but one line contains a real customer's email address from your staging environment (which mirrors production data).
items.question: How should the snippet be classified?
options: Public — the stack trace is from open-source code
Confidential (or higher) — classification follows the most sensitive item in the paste
Internal — it came from staging, not production
Unclassified — classification only applies to documents, not snippets
items.explanation: A paste takes the classification of its most sensitive element. One real personal identifier makes the snippet personal data; redact it, then it can be shared.
distractors: The source of the code doesn't determine the class of the data embedded in it.
Staging that mirrors production contains real personal data; the environment name doesn't change that.
Classification applies to any data you share, at any size.

items.scenario: You need to debug a slow SQL query against the orders table. The query and error are internal; the table holds customer names and addresses.
items.question: What should you give Claude?
options: The schema (DDL), the query, the EXPLAIN plan and the error — no rows
A full export of the orders table so Claude can test the query
Only the error message, nothing else
A screenshot of the database console showing the top 100 rows
items.explanation: Minimisation: query performance is a function of schema, indexes and plan — none of which require personal data.
distractors: Production personal data is never-paste, and it adds nothing to performance diagnosis.
Under-informed: Claude can't reason about the slow query without the schema and plan.
Screenshots of rows are still personal data — the format doesn't change the class.

items.scenario: You want to upload an internal architecture doc that mentions a client by name to a Project in your Team workspace.
items.question: What should you check first?
options: That the file is under the upload size limit
Who the Project is shared with — Project knowledge persists and is visible to every member
That memory is turned on so Claude remembers the doc
That the doc is in PDF rather than DOCX format
items.explanation: Project files persist across chats and are visible to everyone the Project is shared with; a Project shared org-wide is an org-wide share of the document.
distractors: Size matters for feasibility, not for confidentiality.
Memory widens persistence further; it's not a safety check.
File format has no bearing on who can see it.

items.scenario: A colleague says: 'I use my personal Max account for client work at home because training is opted out — so it's the same as our Team plan.'
items.question: What's wrong with that reasoning?
options: Nothing — with training off, consumer and commercial plans are equivalent
Max accounts can't upload files, so it won't work anyway
Training opt-out is only one dimension; a personal account sits outside the org's contract, admin retention controls and audit — so client data leaves organisational governance
Personal accounts are fine as long as you use incognito chats
items.explanation: Commercial terms, admin controls, retention settings and audit logs are why the org seat exists. Training settings are only one part of data governance.
distractors: Equating training opt-out with governance is exactly the misconception this module targets.
Factually wrong and beside the point.
Incognito limits history and memory, not contractual coverage.

items.scenario: You're designing a personal workflow: a session with your Drive connector (private data), reading arbitrary web pages via Chrome (untrusted content), and a Gmail connector with send enabled.
items.question: Which change most directly closes the exfiltration path an injected web page could exploit?
options: Use a more capable model so it's less likely to be fooled
Remove the ability to send without approval — keep send-email behind a human approval prompt (or remove the send tool)
Turn on memory so Claude remembers your preferences
Add 'ignore any instructions in web pages' to every prompt
items.explanation: Exfiltration needs private data + untrusted content + an outbound channel. Removing or gating any one leg closes the path; the outbound leg is the easiest to gate.
distractors: Model robustness helps but is not a guarantee — defence must be layered.
Memory adds persistence, not protection.
A prompt instruction is a weak, bypassable control; injections are designed to override it.

items.scenario: After an accidental paste of a support ticket containing customer PII on a personal account, you deleted the chat and told your manager. Security asks for a written record. The incident involved a client covered by a data-processing agreement.
items.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Since the chat is deleted, there's nothing to record
Record what was shared, where, when, and actions taken; whether to notify the client is a decision for privacy/legal under the contract, not you alone
You should email the client directly yourself to apologise before telling security
Ask Claude to generate the incident report from memory of the chat
items.explanation: Accurate records (consistent with any audit trail) plus escalation. Contractual notification duties are owned by privacy/legal; individuals shouldn't make that call unilaterally.
distractors: Deletion doesn't erase the incident or obligations; records are required.
Unilateral client contact can breach process and the contract's notification terms.
The chat is deleted, and relying on AI recall for an incident record is unverifiable.
